claim: ZRANB1 (human Trabid) missense mutations have been identified in children diagnosed with a range of congenital disorders including reduced brain size.
source: ZRANB1 (human Trabid) missense mutations have been identified in children diagnosed with a range of congenital disorders including reduced brain size, but how Trabid regulates neurodevelopment is not understood.
evidence: Referenced in the abstract as established fact from prior literature

claim: One of the Trabid patient mutations flanked the catalytic cysteine of Trabid and its deubiquitylating (DUB) activity was abrogated.
source: One of the patient mutations flanked the catalytic cysteine of Trabid and its deubiquitylating (DUB) activity was abrogated.
evidence: Supported by in vitro DUB assays shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: The second Trabid variant retained DUB activity, but failed to bind STRIPAK.
source: The second variant retained DUB activity, but failed to bind STRIPAK, a large multiprotein assembly implicated in cytoskeleton organization and neural development.
evidence: Supported by DUB assays and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1

claim: Zranb1 knock-in mice harboring either of these patient mutations exhibited reduced neuronal and glial cell densities in the brain.
source: Zranb1 knock-in mice harboring either of these patient mutations exhibited reduced neuronal and glial cell densities in the brain and a motor deficit consistent with fewer dopaminergic neurons and projections.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Zranb1 knock-in mice harboring either of these patient mutations exhibited a motor deficit consistent with fewer dopaminergic neurons and projections.
source: Zranb1 knock-in mice harboring either of these patient mutations exhibited reduced neuronal and glial cell densities in the brain and a motor deficit consistent with fewer dopaminergic neurons and projections.
evidence: Supported by rotarod performance tests and tyrosine hydroxylase immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3

claim: Both DUB-impaired and STRIPAK-binding-deficient Trabid variants impeded the trafficking of adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) to microtubule plus-ends.
source: Mechanistically, both DUB-impaired and STRIPAK-binding-deficient Trabid variants impeded the trafficking of adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) to microtubule plus-ends.
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figures 5 and 6

claim: The formation of neuronal growth cones and the trajectory of neurite outgrowth from mutant midbrain progenitors were severely compromised.
source: Consequently, the formation of neuronal growth cones and the trajectory of neurite outgrowth from mutant midbrain progenitors were severely compromised.
evidence: Supported by live cell imaging and tracking analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: STRIPAK recruits Trabid to deubiquitylate APC.
source: We propose that STRIPAK recruits Trabid to deubiquitylate APC, and that in cells with mutant Trabid, APC becomes hyperubiquitylated and mislocalized causing impaired organization of the cytoskeleton that underlie the neuronal and developmental phenotypes.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental observations and logical inference

claim: In cells with mutant Trabid, APC becomes hyperubiquitylated and mislocalized causing impaired organization of the cytoskeleton that underlie the neuronal and developmental phenotypes.
source: We propose that STRIPAK recruits Trabid to deubiquitylate APC, and that in cells with mutant Trabid, APC becomes hyperubiquitylated and mislocalized causing impaired organization of the cytoskeleton that underlie the neuronal and developmental phenotypes.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental data from Figures 4, 5, and 6

claim: Trabid exhibits strong DUB specificity for Lys29- and Lys33-linked ubiquitin chains, cleaving these chain types 40-fold more efficiently than Lys63-linked chains.
source: First, it exhibits strong DUB specificity for Lys29- and Lys33-linked ubiquitin chains, cleaving these chain types 40-fold more efficiently than Lys63-linked chains (Licchesi et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from prior published work by Licchesi et al., 2011

claim: Trabid binds the Striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase (STRIPAK) complex.
source: The second defining feature of Trabid is that it binds the Striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase (STRIPAK) complex (Sowa et al., 2009; Tran et al., 2013; Harris et al., 2021), a large multiprotein assembly implicated in cytoskeleton organization, cell migration, and neural development (Hwang and Pallas, 2014; Sakuma et al., 2014; Madsen et al., 2015; Bazzi et al., 2017; Kück et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior published works

claim: STRIPAK is a large multiprotein assembly implicated in cytoskeleton organization, cell migration, and neural development.
source: The second defining feature of Trabid is that it binds the Striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase (STRIPAK) complex (Sowa et al., 2009; Tran et al., 2013; Harris et al., 2021), a large multiprotein assembly implicated in cytoskeleton organization, cell migration, and neural development (Hwang and Pallas, 2014; Sakuma et al., 2014; Madsen et al., 2015; Bazzi et al., 2017; Kück et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior published works

claim: APC has been identified as a candidate Trabid substrate.
source: We have previously identified the APC protein as a candidate Trabid substrate (Tran et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from prior work by the authors

claim: Trabid knockdown in HEK293 cells caused APC to become modified with polyubiquitin and aggregate in the cytoplasm.
source: Trabid knockdown in HEK293 cells caused APC to become modified with polyubiquitin and aggregate in the cytoplasm, whereas high Trabid levels correlated with hypoubiquitylated APC that accumulated in the membrane protrusions of long cell processes.
evidence: Cited from prior work by the authors

claim: High Trabid levels correlated with hypoubiquitylated APC that accumulated in the membrane protrusions of long cell processes.
source: Trabid knockdown in HEK293 cells caused APC to become modified with polyubiquitin and aggregate in the cytoplasm, whereas high Trabid levels correlated with hypoubiquitylated APC that accumulated in the membrane protrusions of long cell processes.
evidence: Cited from prior work by the authors

claim: Trabid regulates the ubiquitylation and subcellular localization of APC.
source: These observations led us to propose that Trabid regulates the ubiquitylation and subcellular localization of APC (Tran et al., 2013).
evidence: Proposed model cited from prior work by the authors

claim: In neurons, APC organizes the cortical cytoskeleton to promote the formation of growth cones and the steering of growing axons that are essential for embryonic brain development.
source: In neurons, APC organizes the cortical cytoskeleton to promote the formation of growth cones and the steering of growing axons that are essential for embryonic brain development (Yokota et al., 2009; Preitner et al., 2014; Dogterom and Koenderink, 2019; Efimova et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior published works

claim: Trabid patient missense mutations R438W and A451V are linked to developmental microcephaly.
source: Trabid/ZRANB1 patient missense mutations, R438W and A451V, are linked to developmental microcephaly (Deciphering Developmental Disorders, 2015).
evidence: Cited from Deciphering Developmental Disorders, 2015

claim: Residue R438 projects prominently into the catalytic cleft formed by the ankyrin repeats and the OTU core of Trabid's catalytic domain.
source: Residue R438 projects prominently into the catalytic cleft formed by the ankyrin repeats and the OTU core of Trabid's catalytic domain (Licchesi et al., 2011), whereas residue A451 resides at the back of the active site, opposite to C443 on alpha helix 4 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Structural analysis based on crystal structure shown in Figure 1B and cited from Licchesi et al., 2011

claim: Residue A451 resides at the back of the active site, opposite to C443 on alpha helix 4.
source: Residue R438 projects prominently into the catalytic cleft formed by the ankyrin repeats and the OTU core of Trabid's catalytic domain (Licchesi et al., 2011), whereas residue A451 resides at the back of the active site, opposite to C443 on alpha helix 4 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Structural analysis shown in Figure 1B

claim: Wild-type Trabid AnkOTU generated appreciable amounts of mono-ubiquitin within 15 min incubation with either Lys29- or Lys63-linked di-ubiquitin chains.
source: Wild-type Trabid AnkOTU generated appreciable amounts of mono-ubiquitin within 15 min incubation with either Lys29- or Lys63-linked di-ubiquitin chains (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro DUB assays shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Trabid R438W showed near total loss of DUB activity, and cleaved ubiquitin product was only readily detected after a prolonged 120 min incubation.
source: In contrast, Trabid R438W showed near total loss of DUB activity, and cleaved ubiquitin product was only readily detected after a prolonged 120 min incubation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro DUB assays shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: A catalytically inactive C443S mutant AnkOTU domain failed to hydrolyze ubiquitin chains even after 2 h incubation.
source: A catalytically inactive C443S mutant AnkOTU domain failed to hydrolyze ubiquitin chains even after 2 h incubation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro DUB assays shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: The Trabid A451V AnkOTU domain cleaved Lys29- or Lys63-linked di-ubiquitin with comparable efficiency to wild-type Trabid.
source: Interestingly, the Trabid A451V AnkOTU domain cleaved Lys29- or Lys63-linked di-ubiquitin with comparable efficiency to wild-type Trabid, despite it being slightly less stable as a recombinant protein based on thermal stability assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro DUB assays shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: The Trabid A451V AnkOTU domain is slightly less stable as a recombinant protein based on thermal stability assay.
source: Interestingly, the Trabid A451V AnkOTU domain cleaved Lys29- or Lys63-linked di-ubiquitin with comparable efficiency to wild-type Trabid, despite it being slightly less stable as a recombinant protein based on thermal stability assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by thermal stability analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: R438W and A451V Trabid AnkOTU proteins retained a functional catalytic interaction with ubiquitin.
source: A ubiquitin suicide probe assay revealed that R438W and A451V Trabid AnkOTU proteins retained a functional catalytic interaction with ubiquitin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitin suicide probe assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Polyubiquitin chains readily co-precipitated with both FLAG-tagged Trabid R438W and C443S expressed in HEK293T cells, consistent with the compromised DUB activity of these mutants.
source: Polyubiquitin chains readily co-precipitated with both FLAG-tagged Trabid R438W and C443S expressed in HEK293T cells, consistent with the compromised DUB activity of these mutants (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1E

claim: The FLAG-Trabid A451V variant did not co-precipitate abundant polyubiquitylated substrates, consistent with it retaining full DUB activity.
source: The FLAG-Trabid A451V variant did not co-precipitate abundant polyubiquitylated substrates, consistent with it retaining full DUB activity (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1E

claim: The FLAG-Trabid A451V mutant failed to efficiently co-precipitate several STRIPAK components, including Striatin3 and STRIP1.
source: Whilst A451V retained full DUB activity, strikingly, in contrast to FLAG-Trabid wild-type, R438W, and C443S, the FLAG-Trabid A451V mutant failed to efficiently co-precipitate several STRIPAK components, including Striatin3 and STRIP1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1E

claim: All FLAG-Trabid proteins co-precipitated similar levels of the substrate E3 ubiquitin ligase HECTD1.
source: All FLAG-Trabid proteins co-precipitated similar levels of the substrate E3 ubiquitin ligase HECTD1 (Tran et al., 2013; Harris et al., 2021).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1E

claim: Mice heterozygous or homozygous for the R438W or A451V mutation were viable, fertile, and born at expected Mendelian ratios.
source: Mice heterozygous or homozygous for the R438W or A451V mutation were viable, fertile, and born at expected Mendelian ratios (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by breeding data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Germline Trabid knockout or C443S homozygous knock-in mice exhibit perinatal lethality.
source: Because germline Trabid knockout or C443S homozygous knock-in mice exhibit perinatal lethality (Dickinson et al., 2016) (our unpublished data), these new R438W and A451V mutant mouse strains allow us to interrogate Trabid function in vivo.
evidence: Cited from Dickinson et al., 2016 and unpublished data

claim: Homozygous mutant mice from the R438W colony weighed on average ~15% less than wild-type littermates.
source: Homozygous mutant mice from the R438W colony weighed on average ~15% less than wild-type littermates, while R438W heterozygous and A451V mutant mice did not exhibit significant weight loss (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by weight measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: R438W heterozygous and A451V mutant mice did not exhibit significant weight loss.
source: Homozygous mutant mice from the R438W colony weighed on average ~15% less than wild-type littermates, while R438W heterozygous and A451V mutant mice did not exhibit significant weight loss (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by weight measurements shown in Figure 2C

claim: Immunohistochemical analysis of brain sections from weaned littermate mice of both mutant strains revealed the normal structure and laminar organization of the cerebral cortex.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of brain sections from weaned littermate mice of both mutant strains revealed the normal structure and laminar organization of the cerebral cortex, but intriguingly a reduction in cell number was apparent in different brain regions of R438W and A451V homozygous mice compared to wild-type littermate controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: A reduction in cell number was apparent in different brain regions of R438W and A451V homozygous mice compared to wild-type littermate controls.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis of brain sections from weaned littermate mice of both mutant strains revealed the normal structure and laminar organization of the cerebral cortex, but intriguingly a reduction in cell number was apparent in different brain regions of R438W and A451V homozygous mice compared to wild-type littermate controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: The number of Ctip2+ medium spiny neurons in the striatum of R438W and A451V mutant mice was reduced compared with wild-type littermates.
source: The number of Ctip2+ medium spiny neurons in the striatum of R438W and A451V mutant mice was reduced compared with wild-type littermates, and homozygous mice showed a greater cell number loss than heterozygous mice, suggesting a gene dosage effect (Figure 2E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2E

claim: Homozygous mice showed a greater cell number loss than heterozygous mice, suggesting a gene dosage effect.
source: The number of Ctip2+ medium spiny neurons in the striatum of R438W and A451V mutant mice was reduced compared with wild-type littermates, and homozygous mice showed a greater cell number loss than heterozygous mice, suggesting a gene dosage effect (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inferred from quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E

claim: R438W and A451V mutant mice had a reduced number of Olig2+ oligodendrocytes in the forebrain and midbrain compared to wild-type littermate mice.
source: Moreover, R438W and A451V mutant mice had a reduced number of Olig2+ oligodendrocytes in the forebrain and midbrain compared to wild-type littermate mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2F

claim: Olig2+ cell numbers in homozygous brain sections were consistently strongly reduced (>30%) compared to wild-type mice, independent of age or sex.
source: Olig2+ cell numbers in homozygous brain sections were consistently strongly reduced (>30%) compared to wild-type mice, independent of age or sex.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of immunohistochemistry data

claim: Of a combined 16 sets of littermate mice from both R438W and A451V colonies, reduced neuronal or glial cell numbers were conspicuous in homozygous brain sections of 12 littermate sets, indicating incomplete penetrance of the mutant phenotype.
source: Of a combined 16 sets of littermate mice from both R438W and A451V colonies, reduced neuronal or glial cell numbers were conspicuous in homozygous brain sections of 12 littermate sets (Figure 2E and F; see also Figure 3), indicating incomplete penetrance of the mutant phenotype.
evidence: Statistical analysis of multiple littermate sets shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: Trabid's DUB and STRIPAK-binding activities are required to produce the correct numbers of neuronal and glial cells in the developing brain.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that Trabid's DUB and STRIPAK-binding activities are required to produce the correct numbers of neuronal and glial cells in the developing brain.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on cell numbers in mutant mice

claim: A reduction in the number of TH+ neurons was observed in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) of Trabid mutant mice from both R438W and A451V colonies, independent of age or sex.
source: A reduction in the number of TH+ neurons was observed in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) of Trabid mutant mice from both R438W and A451V colonies, independent of age or sex (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by tyrosine hydroxylase immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3A

claim: TH immunoreactivity was reduced in the striatum of homozygous R438W and A451V mutant mice.
source: Consistent with the lack of prominent TH+ neuronal processes emanating from the SNc neurons that remain in the mutant midbrain, TH immunoreactivity was reduced in the striatum of homozygous R438W and A451V mutant mice (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by tyrosine hydroxylase immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: The reduced abundance and intensity of TH+ neuronal processes were readily apparent in cortical regions including the motor cortex and claustrum that regulate motor responses.
source: Also in mutant brain sections, the reduced abundance and intensity of TH+ neuronal processes were readily apparent in cortical regions including the motor cortex and claustrum that regulate motor responses (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by tyrosine hydroxylase immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Differences in TH staining in the mutant striatum compared to the wild-type were modest or not observed in all littermates examined, indicating incomplete penetrance of the mutant Trabid alleles.
source: Differences in TH staining in the mutant striatum compared to the wild-type were modest or not observed in all littermates examined (Figure 3D), indicating incomplete penetrance of the mutant Trabid alleles.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of TH staining intensity shown in Figure 3D

claim: Homozygous R438W mice showed a significantly reduced latency to fall at 20, 25, 30, and 35 RPM, compared to controls.
source: Homozygous R438W mice showed a significantly reduced latency to fall at 20, 25, 30, and 35 RPM, compared to controls (Figure 3E), as did homozygous A451V animals at 30 and 35 RPM (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by rotarod performance tests shown in Figure 3E

claim: Homozygous A451V animals showed a significantly reduced latency to fall at 30 and 35 RPM.
source: Homozygous R438W mice showed a significantly reduced latency to fall at 20, 25, 30, and 35 RPM, compared to controls (Figure 3E), as did homozygous A451V animals at 30 and 35 RPM (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by rotarod performance tests shown in Figure 3E

claim: Trabid patient mutations impair motor coordination, consistent with a deficiency in dopaminergic neurons.
source: This indicates that Trabid patient mutations impair motor coordination, consistent with a deficiency in dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: Inferred from rotarod performance and dopaminergic neuron counts

claim: The motor deficit exhibited by both R438W and A451V homozygous mice is likely caused by the abnormal cell numbers and reduced dopaminergic neurons in their brains.
source: However, given that A451V homozygous mice on average are not smaller than wild-type littermates, the motor deficit exhibited by both R438W and A451V homozygous mice is likely caused by the abnormal cell numbers and reduced dopaminergic neurons in their brains (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: Inferred from combined data on body weight, cell numbers, and motor performance

claim: Trabid regulates the brain cellular architecture and neuronal circuitry required for normal motor function.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Trabid regulates the brain cellular architecture and neuronal circuitry required for normal motor function.
evidence: Inferred from combined data on brain histology and motor performance

claim: The levels of ubiquitin-modified APC were strongly suppressed in cells expressing wild-type FLAG-Trabid.
source: The levels of ubiquitin-modified APC were strongly suppressed in cells expressing wild-type FLAG-Trabid (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by GST-TUBE pulldown experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Induction of the FLAG-Trabid R438W mutant, like the catalytically dead FLAG-Trabid C443S, did not repress APC ubiquitylation.
source: In contrast, induction of the FLAG-Trabid R438W mutant, like the catalytically dead FLAG-Trabid C443S, did not repress APC ubiquitylation, and induction of FLAG-Trabid A451V expression only partially reduced APC ubiquitylation compared to control cells (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by GST-TUBE pulldown experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Induction of FLAG-Trabid A451V expression only partially reduced APC ubiquitylation compared to control cells.
source: In contrast, induction of the FLAG-Trabid R438W mutant, like the catalytically dead FLAG-Trabid C443S, did not repress APC ubiquitylation, and induction of FLAG-Trabid A451V expression only partially reduced APC ubiquitylation compared to control cells (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by GST-TUBE pulldown experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: Both DUB and STRIPAK-binding activities of Trabid are required for efficient deubiquitylation of APC in cells.
source: These results suggest that both DUB and STRIPAK-binding activities of Trabid are required for efficient deubiquitylation of APC in cells.
evidence: Inferred from APC ubiquitylation experiments with different Trabid mutants

claim: APC decorates the membrane protrusions at the leading edge of migrating cells.
source: APC decorates the membrane protrusions at the leading edge of migrating cells (Näthke et al., 1996) and we have shown that Trabid is a key regulator of APC localization to these cortical structures (Tran et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from Näthke et al., 1996

claim: Trabid is a key regulator of APC localization to cortical structures at the leading edge of migrating cells.
source: APC decorates the membrane protrusions at the leading edge of migrating cells (Näthke et al., 1996) and we have shown that Trabid is a key regulator of APC localization to these cortical structures (Tran et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior work by the authors (Tran et al., 2013)

claim: FLAG-Trabid localized prominently with EGFP-APC in the tips of long cell processes.
source: Consistent with this insight, FLAG-Trabid localized prominently with EGFP-APC in the tips of long cell processes (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 5A

claim: Analysis of several tip clusters by super-resolution microscopy revealed ~30% overlap between the FLAG-Trabid and EGFP-APC signals.
source: Analysis of several of these tip clusters by super-resolution microscopy revealed ~30% overlap between the FLAG-Trabid and EGFP-APC signals, indicating that a significant fraction of these proteins co-localize in cell tips (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D-SIM super-resolution microscopy shown in Figure 5B

claim: A significant fraction of FLAG-Trabid and EGFP-APC co-localize in cell tips.
source: Analysis of several of these tip clusters by super-resolution microscopy revealed ~30% overlap between the FLAG-Trabid and EGFP-APC signals, indicating that a significant fraction of these proteins co-localize in cell tips (Figure 5B).
evidence: Inferred from super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 5B

claim: In sub-confluent cultures, EGFP-APC localized strongly to the lamellipodial leading edge of the majority of cells co-transfected with wild-type FLAG-Trabid.
source: In sub-confluent cultures, EGFP-APC localized strongly to the lamellipodial leading edge of the majority of cells co-transfected with wild-type FLAG-Trabid (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: In cells co-transfected with the FLAG-Trabid mutants R438W and A451V, EGFP-APC formed irregular punctae at sub-cortical regions close to the leading edge.
source: By contrast, in cells co-transfected with the FLAG-Trabid mutants R438W and A451V, EGFP-APC formed irregular punctae at sub-cortical regions close to the leading edge, and EGFP-APC aggregates are often sequestered to punctae formed by the R438W FLAG-Trabid mutant (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: EGFP-APC aggregates are often sequestered to punctae formed by the R438W FLAG-Trabid mutant.
source: By contrast, in cells co-transfected with the FLAG-Trabid mutants R438W and A451V, EGFP-APC formed irregular punctae at sub-cortical regions close to the leading edge, and EGFP-APC aggregates are often sequestered to punctae formed by the R438W FLAG-Trabid mutant (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: FLAG-Trabid C443S co-localized with EGFP-APC in puncta near the tips of long cell processes.
source: Consistently, FLAG-Trabid C443S co-localized with EGFP-APC in puncta near the tips of long cell processes (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5E

claim: The Trabid substrate HECTD1 was sequestered to C443S punctae in the cytosol, but intriguingly not to punctae residing in proximity of the leading edge membrane.
source: The Trabid substrate HECTD1 was sequestered to C443S punctae in the cytosol, but intriguingly not to punctae residing in proximity of the leading edge membrane (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5E

claim: In near-confluent cultures following prolonged co-transfection of FLAG-Trabid mutants and EGFP-APC, strong EGFP-APC aggregation on or near the plasma membrane and thin tube-like processes extending between neighboring cells decorated with abundant EGFP-APC aggregates of various sizes were observed.
source: In near-confluent cultures following prolonged co-transfection of FLAG-Trabid mutants and EGFP-APC, we observed the striking phenomena of strong EGFP-APC aggregation on or near the plasma membrane and thin tube-like processes extending between neighboring cells decorated with abundant EGFP-APC aggregates of various sizes (Figure 5F).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5F

claim: Trabid's DUB and STRIPAK-binding activities are required for the efficient localization of APC to plasma membrane sites involved in polarised cell migration.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Trabid's DUB and STRIPAK-binding activities are required for the efficient localization of APC to plasma membrane sites involved in polarised cell migration.
evidence: Inferred from APC localization experiments with different Trabid mutants

claim: Endogenous Trabid protein levels were comparable in neural progenitor cultures derived from embryos bearing wild-type or R438W and A451V mutant Trabid alleles.
source: Endogenous Trabid protein levels were comparable in neural progenitor cultures derived from embryos bearing wild-type or R438W and A451V mutant Trabid alleles (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: In neurons with wild-type Trabid, APC-tdTomato accumulated strongly in the tips of growing neurites, marking prominent growth cones that drive axon elongation.
source: In neurons with wild-type Trabid, APC-tdTomato accumulated strongly in the tips of growing neurites, marking prominent growth cones that drive axon elongation (Figure 6C; Zranb1+/+).
evidence: Demonstrated by live cell imaging shown in Figure 6C

claim: In neurons with heterozygous Trabid R438W or A451V mutation, APC-tdTomato exhibited broad distribution along the length of the neurite, and the formation of growth cones was severely compromised.
source: In neurons with heterozygous Trabid R438W or A451V mutation, APC-tdTomato exhibited broad distribution along the length of the neurite, and the formation of growth cones was severely compromised (Figure 6C, Zranb1R438W/+).
evidence: Demonstrated by live cell imaging shown in Figure 6C

claim: Neurites with wild-type Trabid elongated in a polarized manner, whereas neurites with R438W or A451V mutant Trabid turned back or retracted at a greater frequency.
source: Tracking analysis of the turn angles of APC-tdTomato intensities revealed that neurites with wild-type Trabid elongated in a polarized manner, whereas neurites with R438W or A451V mutant Trabid turned back or retracted at a greater frequency (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by tracking analysis shown in Figure 6D and E

claim: Trabid's DUB and STRIPAK-binding activities are required for the efficient transport of APC to neurite tips to promote the formation of growth cones required for polarized axon elongation.
source: These data suggest that Trabid's DUB and STRIPAK-binding activities are required for the efficient transport of APC to neurite tips to promote the formation of growth cones required for polarized axon elongation.
evidence: Inferred from live cell imaging and tracking analysis of APC-tdTomato in neurites

claim: The two patients carrying Trabid missense mutations R438W and A451V were diagnosed with a range of distinct congenital disorders including craniofacial abnormalities, seizures, developmental delay, autism—and both patients presented with microcephaly and constipation.
source: The two patients carrying Trabid missense mutations R438W and A451V were diagnosed with a range of distinct congenital disorders including craniofacial abnormalities, seizures, developmental delay, autism—and both patients presented with microcephaly and constipation (Deciphering Developmental Disorders, 2015).
evidence: Cited from Deciphering Developmental Disorders, 2015

claim: The underlying cause of these seemingly unrelated conditions, broadly classified as neurocristopathies, is the abnormal specification or migration of neural crest cells in the developing embryo.
source: We propose that the underlying cause of these seemingly unrelated conditions, broadly classified as neurocristopathies, is the abnormal specification or migration of neural crest cells in the developing embryo (Vega-Lopez et al., 2018).
evidence: Proposed hypothesis based on patient phenotypes and cited literature

claim: Discrete neural crest populations contribute to the development of craniofacial structures, the forebrain and midbrain, and the enteric nervous system.
source: Discrete neural crest populations contribute to the development of craniofacial structures, the forebrain and midbrain, and the enteric nervous system (Anderson et al., 2006; Creuzet et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from Anderson et al., 2006 and Creuzet et al., 2006

claim: Errors in the formation or polarized migration of neural crest cells could account for all the patient phenotypes, including the reduction in brain volume (microcephaly).
source: Therefore, errors in the formation or polarized migration of neural crest cells could account for all the patient phenotypes, including the reduction in brain volume (microcephaly).
evidence: Speculative inference based on neural crest biology

claim: The irregular cellular architecture and reduced cell numbers in the brains of mice harboring Trabid patient mutations reflect the errant migration of neural crest or neural progenitor cell populations in early embryogenesis.
source: Presently, we can only speculate that the irregular cellular architecture and reduced cell numbers in the brains of mice harboring Trabid patient mutations (Figures 2 and 3) reflect the errant migration of neural crest or neural progenitor cell populations in early embryogenesis (Silva et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative inference based on mouse data and cited literature

claim: Trabid mutant mice showed a motor deficit consistent with the locomotor defects reported for Trabid loss-of-function in Drosophila.
source: While Trabid mutant mice did not exhibit microcephaly, they showed a motor deficit (Figure 3) consistent with the locomotor defects reported for Trabid loss-of-function in Drosophila (Kounatidis et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison of mouse data with cited Drosophila study

claim: The fly Striatin homolog CKA is involved in axonal transport and motor coordination.
source: Intriguingly, the fly Striatin homolog CKA is involved in axonal transport and motor coordination (Neisch et al., 2017), and Drosophila Strip1 regulates endosomal trafficking and axon elongation (Sakuma et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Neisch et al., 2017

claim: Drosophila Strip1 regulates endosomal trafficking and axon elongation.
source: Intriguingly, the fly Striatin homolog CKA is involved in axonal transport and motor coordination (Neisch et al., 2017), and Drosophila Strip1 regulates endosomal trafficking and axon elongation (Sakuma et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Sakuma et al., 2014

claim: Endosomal trafficking defects have been linked to reduced proliferation of neural progenitors and microcephaly.
source: Endosomal trafficking defects have been linked to reduced proliferation of neural progenitors and microcephaly (Carpentieri et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from Carpentieri et al., 2022

claim: Three independent groups have identified Trabid's association with STRIPAK.
source: Three independent groups have identified Trabid's association with STRIPAK (Sowa et al., 2009; Tran et al., 2013; Harris et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from multiple independent studies

claim: The requirement of Trabid binding to STRIPAK for efficient protein trafficking, polarized axon growth, and motor coordination supports the view that Trabid-STRIPAK regulates an evolutionarily conserved mechanism of cell movement required for normal brain development and establishment of the correct neuronal circuitry in the motor system.
source: The requirement of Trabid binding to STRIPAK for efficient protein trafficking, polarized axon growth, and motor coordination (Figures 3, 5 and 6), supports the view that Trabid-STRIPAK regulates an evolutionarily conserved mechanism of cell movement required for normal brain development and establishment of the correct neuronal circuitry in the motor system.
evidence: Inferred from combined experimental data and evolutionary conservation

claim: The impairment of two distinct Trabid functions—polyubiquitin hydrolysis and STRIPAK-binding—led to common cellular, developmental, and behavioral phenotypes, strongly suggesting that these activities act in the same pathway.
source: The impairment of two distinct Trabid functions—polyubiquitin hydrolysis and STRIPAK-binding—led to common cellular, developmental, and behavioral phenotypes (Figures 2—6; Deciphering Developmental Disorders, 2015), strongly suggesting that these activities act in the same pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of phenotypes caused by different mutations

claim: APC is the primary molecular target of Trabid action in cytoskeleton organization and polarized axon growth.
source: We propose that APC is the primary molecular target of Trabid action in cytoskeleton organization and polarized axon growth (Figure 7).
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data

claim: APC is an established regulator of cell adhesion and migration, and it governs the cortical actin and microtubule cytoskeleton dynamics required to form and steer axonal growth cones.
source: APC is an established regulator of cell adhesion and migration, and it governs the cortical actin and microtubule cytoskeleton dynamics required to form and steer axonal growth cones (Dogterom and Koenderink, 2019; Efimova et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Dogterom and Koenderink, 2019 and Efimova et al., 2020

claim: Trabid and Striatin interacted with the armadillo repeat domain (ARD) of APC, but not with an APC ARD mutant that caused cell-cell adhesion defects.
source: In a yeast two-hybrid screen, we found that Trabid and Striatin interacted with the armadillo repeat domain (ARD) of APC, but not with an APC ARD mutant that caused cell-cell adhesion defects (Hamada and Bienz, 2002; Tran et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from prior work by the authors and Hamada and Bienz, 2002

claim: A functional interaction between Trabid, Striatin, and APC promotes the fidelity of cell-cell or cell-substratum contacts.
source: This implies that a functional interaction between Trabid, Striatin, and APC promotes the fidelity of cell-cell or cell-substratum contacts.
evidence: Inferred from yeast two-hybrid data and APC mutant phenotypes

claim: Trabid complexes with Striatin/STRIPAK in human cell lines.
source: Our model of Trabid action in Figure 7 integrates published data showing that (1) Trabid complexes with Striatin/STRIPAK in human cell lines (Sowa et al., 2009; Tran et al., 2013; Harris et al., 2021), and (2) Striatin binds directly to the ARD domain of APC (Breitman et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior studies

claim: Striatin binds directly to the ARD domain of APC.
source: Our model of Trabid action in Figure 7 integrates published data showing that (1) Trabid complexes with Striatin/STRIPAK in human cell lines (Sowa et al., 2009; Tran et al., 2013; Harris et al., 2021), and (2) Striatin binds directly to the ARD domain of APC (Breitman et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from Breitman et al., 2008

claim: Trabid and/or Striatin deficiency caused APC hyperubiquitylation and aggregation, perturbed actin assembly and microtubule stability, and inhibited the migration of mouse and human cell lines.
source: Consistent with this model, Trabid and/or Striatin deficiency caused APC hyperubiquitylation and aggregation, perturbed actin assembly and microtubule stability, and inhibited the migration of mouse and human cell lines (Bai et al., 2011; Tran et al., 2013) (our unpublished data).
evidence: Cited from prior published work and unpublished data

claim: Ubiquitin-modified APC correlated with its binding to Axin in the β-catenin destruction complex.
source: We have shown that ubiquitin-modified APC correlated with its binding to Axin in the β-catenin destruction complex (Tran and Polakis, 2012), whereas non-ubiquitin-modified APC accumulates in membrane protrusions (Tran et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior work by the authors

claim: Non-ubiquitin-modified APC accumulates in membrane protrusions.
source: We have shown that ubiquitin-modified APC correlated with its binding to Axin in the β-catenin destruction complex (Tran and Polakis, 2012), whereas non-ubiquitin-modified APC accumulates in membrane protrusions (Tran et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from prior work by the authors

claim: Reversible modification with polyubiquitin could be the long-hypothesized molecular switch that regulates the distribution of APC between its many functional pools in cells.
source: Thus, reversible modification with polyubiquitin could be the long-hypothesized molecular switch that regulates the distribution of APC between its many functional pools in cells (Dikovskaya et al., 2001; Bienz, 2002).
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental data and cited literature

claim: Chronic APC ubiquitylation in Trabid deficient/mutant cells might result in increased APC sequestration into Axin destruction complexes or promote spurious interactions with ubiquitin-binding proteins that retard APC trafficking along microtubules.
source: Chronic APC ubiquitylation in Trabid deficient/mutant cells might result in increased APC sequestration into Axin destruction complexes or promote spurious interactions with ubiquitin-binding proteins that retard APC trafficking along microtubules.
evidence: Speculative mechanism based on experimental observations

claim: Rescue of the APC transport defect could hypothetically be achieved by inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3), which abolishes APC ubiquitylation.
source: Rescue of the APC transport defect could hypothetically be achieved by inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3), which we have shown abolishes APC ubiquitylation (Tran and Polakis, 2012).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on prior work showing GSK3 effect on APC ubiquitylation

claim: GSK3 inactivation promotes the association of APC with microtubule plus-ends to drive polarized cell migration.
source: Supporting this idea is the finding that GSK3 inactivation promotes the association of APC with microtubule plus-ends to drive polarized cell migration (Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2003).
evidence: Cited from Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2003

claim: Optimal cell migration and adhesion require stable, acetylated microtubules.
source: Optimal cell migration and adhesion require stable, acetylated microtubules (Aguilar et al., 2014; Bance et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from Aguilar et al., 2014 and Bance et al., 2019

claim: The loss of APC and the STRIPAK proteins STRIP1 and CTTNBP2 strongly reduced the acetylated microtubule network in neurons.
source: Of note, the loss of APC and the STRIPAK proteins STRIP1 and CTTNBP2 strongly reduced the acetylated microtubule network in neurons (Yokota et al., 2009; Shih et al., 2014; Sakuma et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior studies

claim: Striatin depletion perturbed cell-cell adhesion.
source: Furthermore, Striatin depletion perturbed cell-cell adhesion (Breitman et al., 2008; Lahav-Ariel et al., 2019) and axon elongation defects caused by STRIP1 mutation are linked to the dysregulation of neuronal adhesion (Sakuma et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Breitman et al., 2008 and Lahav-Ariel et al., 2019

claim: Axon elongation defects caused by STRIP1 mutation are linked to the dysregulation of neuronal adhesion.
source: Furthermore, Striatin depletion perturbed cell-cell adhesion (Breitman et al., 2008; Lahav-Ariel et al., 2019) and axon elongation defects caused by STRIP1 mutation are linked to the dysregulation of neuronal adhesion (Sakuma et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from Sakuma et al., 2014

claim: Chronic APC ubiquitylation and dysfunction may underlie all Trabid and STRIPAK mutant phenotypes.
source: It would be interesting to investigate if chronic APC ubiquitylation and dysfunction underlie all Trabid and STRIPAK mutant phenotypes.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis for future investigation

claim: Lys29-linked polyubiquitin exists mainly as heterotypic chains containing Lys48 linkages that target substrates for degradation.
source: Lys29-linked polyubiquitin exists mainly as heterotypic chains containing Lys48 linkages that target substrates for degradation (Kristariyanto et al., 2015; Leto et al., 2019; Harris et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from multiple prior studies

claim: Trabid is thought to modulate the levels of Lys29/Lys48 mixed chains to regulate proteostasis, autophagy, and cell division.
source: Trabid is thought to modulate the levels of Lys29/Lys48 mixed chains to regulate proteostasis, autophagy, and cell division (Chen et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021; Vaughan et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from multiple recent studies

claim: Lys33-linked ubiquitin polymers have been implicated in post-Golgi protein trafficking.
source: Lys33-linked ubiquitin polymers have been implicated in post-Golgi protein trafficking (Yuan et al., 2014), and Lys63-linked chains are abundant cellular adducts with established roles in the sorting of endosomal/lysosomal cargo (Erpapazoglou et al., 2014) and mediating the formation of protein assemblies (Tran and Polakis, 2012).
evidence: Cited from Yuan et al., 2014

claim: Lys63-linked chains are abundant cellular adducts with established roles in the sorting of endosomal/lysosomal cargo and mediating the formation of protein assemblies.
source: Lys33-linked ubiquitin polymers have been implicated in post-Golgi protein trafficking (Yuan et al., 2014), and Lys63-linked chains are abundant cellular adducts with established roles in the sorting of endosomal/lysosomal cargo (Erpapazoglou et al., 2014) and mediating the formation of protein assemblies (Tran and Polakis, 2012).
evidence: Cited from Erpapazoglou et al., 2014 and Tran and Polakis, 2012

claim: High expression of Trabid, APC, and STRIPAK proteins in neural stem cells indicate that Trabid's association with STRIPAK and its ability to regulate APC polyubiquitylation may be important for neurogenesis.
source: High expression of Trabid, APC, and STRIPAK proteins in neural stem cells (Castets et al., 2000; Blanpain et al., 2004; Yokota et al., 2009) indicate that Trabid's association with STRIPAK and its ability to regulate APC polyubiquitylation may be important for neurogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from expression patterns cited from prior studies

claim: The neuronal and developmental phenotypes associated with Trabid loss-of-function mutations are primarily caused by the mislocalization of APC that leads to defective cytoskeleton organization and aberrant cell locomotion.
source: We propose that the neuronal and developmental phenotypes associated with these Trabid loss-of-function mutations are primarily caused by the mislocalization of APC that leads to defective cytoskeleton organization and aberrant cell locomotion.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data

claim: DUBs catalyze the removal of ubiquitin from protein substrates to regulate protein stability, activity, interaction, or localization.
source: DUBs catalyze the removal of ubiquitin from protein substrates to regulate protein stability, activity, interaction, or localization (Komander et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from Komander et al., 2009

claim: Ubiquitin can be assembled into polymers linked through one of eight internal ubiquitin residues – Met1, Lys6, Lys11, Lys27, Lys29, Lys33, Lys48, and Lys63.
source: Ubiquitin can be assembled into polymers linked through one of eight internal ubiquitin residues – Met1, Lys6, Lys11, Lys27, Lys29, Lys33, Lys48, and Lys63 – and impairment of DUB function can lead to the accumulation of one or more of these ubiquitin chain linkages on a protein substrate with deleterious consequences.
evidence: Established knowledge in the ubiquitin field

claim: LINKED syndrome is a human syndrome caused by loss-of-function mutations in the DUB OTUD5, associated with increased Lys48-linked ubiquitylation and turnover of chromatin remodeling and transcription factors that are critical for normal embryonic development.
source: For example, LINKage-specific deubiquitylation deficiency-induced Embryonic Defects (LINKED), a human syndrome caused by loss-of-function mutations in the DUB OTUD5, is associated with increased Lys48-linked ubiquitylation and turnover of chromatin remodeling and transcription factors that are critical for normal embryonic development (Beck et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Beck et al., 2021

claim: LINKED syndrome patients manifest severe congenital malformations and die in early infancy.
source: Consequently, LINKED syndrome patients manifest severe congenital malformations and die in early infancy (Beck et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Beck et al., 2021

claim: OTUD5 belongs to a 17-member family of human DUBs that possess an OTU (ovarian tumor) catalytic domain and include the closely related OTU DUBs A20, Cezanne, and Trabid.
source: OTUD5 belongs to a 17-member family of human DUBs that possess an OTU (ovarian tumor) catalytic domain and include the closely related OTU DUBs A20, Cezanne, and Trabid.
